newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels meet with mediators at besieged embassy.
newsitem.headline: Rebels meet with mediators at besieged embassy.

text.p: Two mediators in Peru's 82-day hostage crisis met with Marxist guerrillas in the Japanese ambassador's residence on Sunday to try to get stalled negotiations to end the standoff back on track.

Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canadian envoy Anthony Vincent, both members of a three-man guarantors commission, walked into the ambassador's mansion, with Cipriani wheeling a small suitcase behind him, and left about two hours later.
They said later discussions would continue on Monday but gave no hint as to whether face-to-face talks between the government and the rebels were any closer.
"Our message today is that the discussions will continue tomorrow. In the next week, the discussions should be important ones," Vincent told reporters.
"We ask everyone involved to let these conversations continue in the way they have, seeking a solution that, although difficult, is viable," Cipriani told reporters later.
Their visit to the besieged residence gave the first sign, however tenuous, that talks could resume between the government and rebels after collapsing last week.

The two men paid no heed to a noisy street rally by a few hundred supporters of President Alberto Fujimori shouting for freedom for the 72 hostages and demanding the government concede nothing to the rebels.
"Don't give in one inch, the people want peace!" shouted the demonstrators, loud enough for rebels and hostages inside the diplomatic compound to hear.

Not counting a visit by Cipriani alone on Saturday, the meeting marked the first direct contact between the commission and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels since they angrily charged Fujimori with planning to take the residence by storm and severed talks on Thursday.

Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa earlier said his group, who blasted their way into the residence on Dec. 17 during a cocktail party, would listen to the mediators but wasn't sure if or when MRTA would return to the bargaining table.
"We'll wait for the guarantors commision to come here, talk to them and, at that point, we'll decide," he said in a walkie- talkie interview. "We are constantly evaluating the situation."
MRTA, a Cuban-style guerrilla group believed almost wiped out until it roared back to life with the siege, is demanding freedom for 458 captured comrades from jail in exchange for the hostages.

Fujimori has said he will never concede on that point but has shown flexibility in a few other areas, flying to Cuba last week to arrange asylum for at least some of the rebels if they release the hostages.

A Japanese daily reported on Sunday that the government has proposed letting most of the 20-odd rebels in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima remain in the country if they release of all their captives.
The Mainichi Shimbun quoted sources close to Fujimori and his negotiating team as saying the proposal was submitted on Wednesday during the last round of talks between the government and MRTA.

The paper said officials proposed letting most of the rebels stay in Peru without prosecution, provided Cerpa and up to three others charged with prior offences went into exile in Cuba. It also offered to make prison and judicial reforms and changes in the way criminal investigations are undertaken.
Fujimori and his allies have refused to rule out using force to free the hostages, even as they move closer to resuming negotiations.

"If these conversations don't bring any results, what is the government going to do? It has to be prepared to act, using all instruments it considers necessary," said a key political ally of Fujimori, congressman Carlos Torres y Torres Lara.
"The government ... will impose its will when that becomes necessary," he said in a television interview.

The atmosphere outside the walled compound had an almost comic feel on Sunday. Friends of the hostages drove past in a long line of Volkswagen beetles, tooting their horns in unison with the words "Long live peace" written on their windscreens, and street hawkers sold T-shirts saying "Just go home Nestor!!", a reference to Cerpa.
The 72 captives are all housed on two floors of the building with no electricity and limited water supplies.

With the windows closed and no air conditioning amid one of Lima's hottest summers in memory, the hostages must be very uncomfortable and about 20 of them are in various stages of illness, local media has reported. Red Cross doctors are occasionally let inside to treat the sick.
